answer:
HYPOTHESIS (candidate natural-language answer to "How does the median wealth of white individuals compare to that of black and Hispanic individuals from 1985 onwards?"):

"Among NLSY79 respondents, the median family net wealth of white (non-Black non-Hispanic) individuals exceeded that of both Black and Hispanic individuals in every survey wave from 1985 onwards, and the gap widened dramatically over time. In 1985 white respondents' median wealth ($3,500) was about 2.2× the Black median ($1,600) and 7× the Hispanic median ($500); by 1990 it had grown to 2.7× the Black median ($12,972 vs $4,800) and 8.1× the Hispanic median ($1,600); and by 1996 it reached 4.35× the Black median ($42,600 vs $9,800) and 16.6× the Hispanic median ($42,600 vs $2,562). In dollar terms the white–Black gap grew from $1,900 (1985) to $8,172 (1990) to $32,800 (1996), and the white–Hispanic gap from $3,000 to $11,372 to $40,038 — i.e., white median wealth grew roughly twelvefold between 1985 and 1996 while Black median wealth grew about sixfold and Hispanic median wealth only about fivefold, so racial/ethnic wealth disparities widened both absolutely and relatively over this period."

EXECUTED RESULTS

Table 1 — Median family net wealth by cohort per wave (non-missing wealth only; zeros and negatives retained):

| Year | Cohort | Valid N | Median | % negative | % zero |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1985 | Black | 1,699 | $1,600 | 10.8% | 17.7% |
| 1985 | Hispanic | 2,631 | $500 | 10.9% | 31.0% |
| 1985 | white (non-Black non-Hispanic) | 5,774 | $3,500 | 12.6% | 6.6% |
| 1990 | Black | 1,528 | $4,800 | 15.4% | 10.1% |
| 1990 | Hispanic | 2,431 | $1,600 | 14.3% | 19.5% |
| 1990 | white (non-Black non-Hispanic) | 5,336 | $12,972 | 12.5% | 4.0% |
| 1996 | Black | 1,368 | $9,800 | 10.7% | 10.1% |
| 1996 | Hispanic | 2,114 | $2,562 | 12.4% | 22.4% |
| 1996 | white (non-Black non-Hispanic) | 3,557 | $42,600 | 8.5% | 2.4% |

Table 2 — White-vs-group gaps per wave (numbers that feed the hypothesis sentence, traced):

| Year | Comparison | Ratio (white ÷ group) | Dollar diff (white − group) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1985 | white vs Black | 2.19× | +$1,900 |
| 1985 | white vs Hispanic | 7.00× | +$3,000 |
| 1990 | white vs Black | 2.70× | +$8,172 |
| 1990 | white vs Hispanic | 8.11× | +$11,372 |
| 1996 | white vs Black | 4.35× | +$32,800 |
| 1996 | white vs Hispanic | 16.62× | +$40,038 |

TRACEABILITY — which numbers feed which hypothesis claims:
- "exceeded in every wave": every white median > Black and > Hispanic median in Tables 1/2 (6/6 comparisons).
- "2.2× / 7× (1985), 2.7× / 8.1× (1990), 4.35× / 16.6× (1996)": Table 2 ratio column.
- "$1,900→$8,172→$32,800 (white–Black)" and "$3,000→$11,372→$40,038 (white–Hispanic)": Table 2 dollar_diff column.
- "white grew ~12×, Black ~6×, Hispanic ~5×": Table 1 medians (3,500→42,600 = 12.2×; 1,600→9,800 = 6.1×; 500→2,562 = 5.1×).
- Trend statement (one line): The white-vs-Black and white-vs-Hispanic median-wealth gaps widened monotonically across 1985→1990→1996 in both relative (2.2×→2.7×→4.4× and 7.0×→8.1×→16.6×) and absolute ($1.9k→$8.2k→$32.8k and $3.0k→$11.4k→$40.0k) terms.

CONTEXT (share negative/zero, Table 1's last two columns): Black and Hispanic cohorts carry substantially more zero/negative wealth than the white cohort in every wave (e.g., 1996: Hispanic 22.4% zero vs white 2.4%), which is why the Hispanic median stays near zero and makes the ratio gap especially sensitive.

CAVEATS (carried from the approved plan):
- Attrition: valid N per wave falls relative to the 1979 cohort sizes — Black 1,699/1,528/1,368 of 2,002; Hispanic 2,631/2,431/2,114 of 3,174; white 5,774/5,336/3,557 of 7,510. The 1996 wave loses the most respondents (white attrition is proportionally largest), so late-wave estimates are based on a shrinking, possibly selective sample.
- Non-ignorable missingness: wealth non-response is unlikely to be random across cohorts or wealth levels; cross-cohort medians could be biased by differential non-response. Not correctable with the variables in this file.
- "White" is a proxy for cohort code 3 (non-Black non-Hispanic), which also includes Asians and other groups; the proxy label is kept visible in all output.
- Unweighted sample medians (no survey weights in file); "1985 onwards" is covered only by the three available waves (1985, 1990, 1996), unevenly spaced.
- Negative net wealth values are real (assets-minus-debts construction; asset components in the file are never negative) and were retained in all medians.

METHOD (exactly as approved, no imputation, no extra modeling): per-wave median of non-missing `Family net wealth` by `Racial/ethnic cohort, 1979` ({1→Black, 2→Hispanic, 3→white (non-Black non-Hispanic)}); zeros and negatives retained; gaps reported as both ratio (white median ÷ group median) and dollar difference (white − group). Executed script: analysis/wealth_gap_analysis.py; printed output: analysis/wealth_gap_output.txt.

payload.hypothesis: Among NLSY79 respondents, the median family net wealth of white (non-Black non-Hispanic) individuals exceeded that of both Black and Hispanic individuals in every survey wave from 1985 onwards, and the gap widened dramatically over time: white median wealth was 2.2x the Black median and 7x the Hispanic median in 1985 ($3,500 vs $1,600 and $500), 2.7x and 8.1x in 1990 ($12,972 vs $4,800 and $1,600), and 4.35x and 16.6x in 1996 ($42,600 vs $9,800 and $2,562); in dollar terms the white-Black gap grew from $1,900 to $8,172 to $32,800 and the white-Hispanic gap from $3,000 to $11,372 to $40,038, i.e., white median wealth grew roughly twelvefold between 1985 and 1996 while Black median wealth grew about sixfold and Hispanic median wealth about fivefold, so racial/ethnic wealth disparities widened both absolutely and relatively over the period.
payload.workflow: Loaded data/nls_raw.csv (12,686 rows); mapped Racial/ethnic cohort, 1979 {1=Black, 2=Hispanic, 3=white (non-Black non-Hispanic, proxy)}; computed per-wave medians of Family net wealth (1985, 1990, 1996) on non-missing values only, retaining zeros and negatives; reported valid N, share negative and share zero per cohort-year; computed white-vs-Black and white-vs-Hispanic gaps as both ratios and dollar differences per wave; no imputation, no weights, no modeling.
